pos: n. (c. 1510–1545; Lithuanian humanist and reformer, founder of the first higher school in Vilnius, driven into exile for the gospel)
etymology: Kulvietis, from the Lithuanian estate name Kulva; latinised as Culvensis, the man of Kulva.
biblical_def: Abraomas Kulvietis was a Lithuanian nobleman who studied at Cracow, Louvain, Leipzig and Wittenberg, took his doctorate in law at Siena, and came home in 1539 to open at Vilnius the first school of higher learning Lithuania had ever had. Some sixty sons of the nobility were taught there. He preached the gospel plainly and had Queen Bona's protection for a while; in 1542 Bishop Paulius Alsenietis moved against him, the school was shut, and Kulvietis fled to Prussia, where Duke Albert made him professor of Greek and Hebrew at Königsberg. He wrote his Confessio fidei there, the first Lithuanian Protestant confession, addressed to the queen who had failed to shield him. He came back to Lithuania in 1545 under a toleration edict and died within months, aged about thirty-five. The dictionary records him for the thing he would not do, which was be quiet: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as the acknowledgment of a crime or of a belief, a formulary of articles of faith; exile as banishment, the state of being driven from one's country; and a testimony as a solemn declaration, in Scripture the divine law.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. [L. confessio.] The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something to one's disadvantage; a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; the person banished.
TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration or affirmation; in Scripture, the divine law, the two tables, the whole divine revelation.
SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.
BOND, n. Anything that binds; a cord, a chain; an obligation; imprisonment, captivity.
scriptures: I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
corruption_summary: Lithuanian reformer who founded the first higher school in Vilnius in 1539, was driven out by the bishop in 1542, taught Greek and Hebrew at Königsberg, and wrote the first Lithuanian Protestant confession.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Kulvietis is sometimes claimed as a figure of national awakening and nothing else, a founder of Lithuanian letters whose religion was incidental to his patriotism. The order was the other way round. He learned Greek and Hebrew to read the Scriptures, taught them so that others could, and wrote his confession to a queen because he expected to be judged for what he believed and not for what he had built.

The principle to recover is that a scattering does not stop the word; it carries it. The pattern in Acts is not survival but advance: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). Paul in prison makes the same distinction between the preacher's circumstances and the word's liberty — “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9) — and the Psalm sets the posture for a man summoned before power with his Bible in his hand: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46). Hebrews gives the world's valuation of such men and corrects it in a parenthesis: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:)” (Heb 11:38).

pos: n. (c. 1500–1545; Lithuanian theologian, first professor of theology at Königsberg)
etymology: Rapolionis, from the Lithuanian place name Rapolionys; latinised as Rapagelanus.
biblical_def: Stanislovas Rapolionis was a Lithuanian of the lesser nobility who studied at Cracow and then, with Albert's stipend, at Wittenberg, where he took his doctorate in theology in 1544 under Luther himself. He was at once made the first professor of theology in the new Königsberg university, the senior theological chair in the duchy, and he held it for scarcely a year before he died in 1545. In that year he lectured on the Psalms, disputed against purgatory, and began turning hymns and the Lord's Prayer into Lithuanian. Luther and Melanchthon both thought highly of him; Mazvydas and Vilentas were his students. He is the first academic theologian his nation produced, and he spent his teaching on putting the faith into a tongue that had no printed Christian book at all. Paul's chain of questions is his biography: “and how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects; to interpret as to explain the meaning of words to one who does not understand them; and distinctly as with clearness, plainly, without confusion.
webster_full: PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one that inculcates anything with earnestness.
INTERPRET, v.t. [L. interpretor.] To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them; to translate into intelligible terms.
DISTINCTLY, adv. With distinctness; not confusedly; plainly; clearly; without the blending of one part with another.
PROFESSOR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; one that occupies a chair in a university.
SENSE, n. [L. sensus.] Meaning; import; signification; the sense of a word or passage.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
corruption_summary: First professor of theology at Königsberg, 1544; Luther's doctoral student, teacher of Mazvydas, and the first to render Lithuanian hymns and the Lord's Prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a quieter error worth naming: the assumption that a man who dies after one year in post has left nothing. Rapolionis held his chair for about twelve months. What came out of it was the generation that printed Lithuania's first books. The dictionary records him because fruitfulness is not measured by the length of a tenure, and because a teacher is paid in other men's work.

The principle to recover is that preaching, sending and understanding are one chain and cannot be unlinked. Paul reasons backwards from the hearer to the sender, asking first “and how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14), and then pressing one step further back to the commission itself: “And how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15). The preaching itself must be intelligible or it is not preaching: Nehemiah's Levites “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8), and Paul puts the alternative bluntly — “for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). A sermon in a tongue the congregation does not possess is speech aimed at nobody.

pos: n. (c. 1510–1563; author of the first printed book in the Lithuanian language, pastor at Ragnit)
etymology: Mazvydas, a Lithuanian surname; latinised as Mosvidius. Martynas, from Latin Martinus, of Mars.
biblical_def: Martynas Mazvydas was brought from Lithuania to Königsberg by Duke Albert in 1546, matriculated at the university, and the next year produced Catechismusa prasty szadei — the plain words of the catechism — printed at Königsberg on 8 January 1547. It is the first book ever printed in Lithuanian: a primer, a catechism, eleven hymns with tunes, and a verse preface addressed to the Lithuanian and Samogitian parishes, telling them to take the book and read. He was ordained and sent as pastor to Ragnit on the Prussian side of the Nemunas, where he served sixteen years, preaching to Lithuanian-speaking congregations and compiling the hymnal his cousin Vilentas finished after his death. The dictionary records him because a nation's first printed sentence was a catechism question, and because of Paul's verdict on worship in an unknown tongue: “I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer, particularly in the principles of religion; a primer as a small elementary book for teaching children; and a barbarian as a foreigner, one whose speech is not understood.
webster_full: CATECHISM, n. [Gr. katechismos.] A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
PRIMER, n. A small elementary book for teaching children to read; a first book.
BARBARIAN, n. [Gr. barbaros.] A man in his rude, savage state; among the Greeks and Romans, a foreigner, one whose language was not understood.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; a language; the speech or dialect of a particular nation.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach and form by practice; to exercise and discipline.
scriptures: Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: Author of Catechismusa prasty szadei, printed at Königsberg in January 1547, the first book in the Lithuanian language; pastor at Ragnit for sixteen years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a flattening of what the book was. Mazvydas's catechism is treated as a monument of philology, the oldest specimen of written Lithuanian, and so it is; it is quarried for grammar and spelling. But it was made to be used by parents and parish clerks on people who could not read, and its verse preface is a direct address to peasants, not to scholars. A first book that is a catechism tells you what the men who made it thought the alphabet was for.

The principle to recover is that God means to be understood in the mother tongue, and that Pentecost settled it. The wonder the crowd reports is not that the apostles were eloquent but that the hearing was native: “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8). Without that, Paul says, preacher and hearer are mutual foreigners — “I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11). And the instruction is domestic before it is academic, laid on fathers in the house and on the road: “And ye shall teach them your children” (Deu 11:19).

pos: n. (1536–1602; Lithuanian pastor and chronicler who translated the whole Bible into Lithuanian and never saw it printed)
etymology: Bretkūnas, from the German surname Bretke; Jonas, the Lithuanian form of Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Jonas Bretkūnas was born near Friedland in Prussian Lithuania, studied at Königsberg, Wittenberg and probably Tübingen, and served as pastor at Labiau from 1563 and at the Lithuanian church in Königsberg from 1587. Besides a hymnal, a postil of seventy-one sermons, and a chronicle of Prussia, he did what no one in his nation had attempted: between 1579 and 1590 he translated the entire Bible into Lithuanian, working from Luther's German with the Vulgate and the Greek beside him, and finished it in eleven years. The manuscript was handed to the ducal government for printing and the printing never happened. It was read, borrowed, copied from, and shelved; it survives in eight volumes and was first published in full in the twentieth century. The dictionary records him as the pattern of unrewarded labour on a thing that cannot perish: “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to translate as to interpret, to render into another language; a manuscript as a book or paper written with the hand, not printed; and to endure as to last, to continue in the same state without perishing.
webster_full: TRANSLATE, v.t. [L. translatus.] To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
MANUSCRIPT, n. [L. manu scriptus.] A book or paper written with the hand, or pen, and not printed.
ENDURE, v.i. To last; to continue in the same state without perishing; to remain; to abide.
WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its natural freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
VISION, n. [L. visio.] The act of seeing; a revelation from God; something imparted by supernatural means.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever.
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
corruption_summary: Lithuanian pastor who translated the whole Bible into Lithuanian between 1579 and 1590; the manuscript was submitted for printing and never printed in his lifetime.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a genuine temptation the entry should name, because Bretkūnas is the standing refutation of it: the temptation to reckon a work worthless because it was not published. Eleven years, eight volumes, a whole canon, and no printed book. The dictionary observes that the manuscript nevertheless taught Lithuanian prose to the men who came after, supplied later translators their vocabulary, and preserved a sixteenth-century tongue that would otherwise be largely lost.

The principle to recover is that the permanence belongs to the word and not to the edition. Isaiah sets the two side by side without flattery to the labourer: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). The Psalm dates that permanence from the start and not from a printing privilege — “Thy word is true from the beginning” (Psa 119:160). Habakkuk is nevertheless ordered to write it legibly and large, for a reader who is in a hurry: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). The command is to make it plain; the publishing is God's business.

pos: n. (c. 1525–1587; Lithuanian pastor at Königsberg, translator of the Gospels and Epistles and of Luther's small catechism)
etymology: Vilentas, a Lithuanian surname of uncertain derivation; Baltramiejus, the Lithuanian form of Bartholomew, son of Talmai.
biblical_def: Baltramiejus Vilentas was Mazvydas's kinsman and fellow student, came with him to Königsberg in the 1540s, and from 1550 served as pastor of the Lithuanian congregation in the city for nearly forty years. He finished and published the hymnal Mazvydas left incomplete, and in 1579 printed two books of his own: an Enchiridion, Luther's small catechism in Lithuanian, and Euangelias bei Epistolas, the gospel and epistle readings for the church year, which is the first Lithuanian book of Scripture texts. He defended his translations against charges of error, insisted that a plain parish needed the readings in its own speech more than it needed a learned preacher, and encouraged Bretkūnas in the full translation. The dictionary records him because he aimed at certainty in ordinary people: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines certainty as a fixed and real state, exemption from doubt or failure; an epistle as a writing communicated from one person to another, a letter; and to search as to look over carefully in order to find something.
webster_full: CERTAINTY, n. [L. certus.] A fixed and real state; exemption from failure; full assurance of mind; freedom from doubt.
EPISTLE, n. [Gr. epistole.] A writing, directed or sent, communicating intelligence to a distant person; a letter.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to examine by inspection.
ENCHIRIDION, n. [Gr. en, in, and cheir, the hand.] A manual; a book carried in the hand for ready use.
READY, a. Prompt; quick; not slow or dull; willing; free and cheerful to do a thing.
scriptures: Luk 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Col 4:16
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Pastor of the Lithuanian congregation at Königsberg for nearly forty years; published Luther's small catechism and the gospel and epistle readings in Lithuanian in 1579.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to resist here is the notion that lectionary work is clerical busywork. Vilentas printed the readings for the church year because a congregation that hears the same portions, in order, year by year, in its own tongue, is being catechised whether or not the preacher is able. That is a deliberate strategy for a church with too few trained men, and it is the opposite of a formality.

The principle to recover is that Scripture aims at certainty and submits to examination to get it. Luke writes so that a reader already instructed may know: “That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:4). The Bereans are commended for the very thing a false teacher most dislikes, checking the preacher against the text: “and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). Paul orders his letters passed between congregations and read aloud (Col 4:16), and Timothy's knowledge of the holy Scriptures began in childhood (2Ti 3:15). None of that works in a language the people do not have.

pos: n. (c. 1482–1567; printer and pastor at Lyck in Prussian Masuria, translator of the catechism into Polish)
etymology: Małecki, a Polish surname from mały, small; latinised as Maletius.
biblical_def: Jan Małecki was a Cracow printer who turned evangelical, moved into ducal Prussia, and about 1536 set up a press at Lyck in Masuria, the Polish-speaking corner of the duchy. He printed Polish books for the Masurian parishes, translated Luther's catechism into Polish, and served as pastor and then superintendent at Lyck; his son Hieronim succeeded him in both the press and the pulpit and carried the work on. He quarrelled with Mazvydas and with others over renderings and over jurisdiction, and the records show a difficult man. He also put a printed catechism into the hands of a population that had none, in a region no one else was serving, and kept at it for thirty years. The dictionary records him for the generational logic of the work: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a printer as one who prints books or papers; a generation as a single succession of men in the line of descent; and to commit as to entrust, to give in charge or trust.
webster_full: PRINTER, n. One who prints books, pamphlets or papers; one that impresses letters and words upon paper.
GENERATION, n. [L. generatio.] A single succession of men or animals in natural descent; the people of the same period.
COMMIT, v.t. [L. committo.] To give in trust; to put into the hands or power of another; to entrust.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
SHEW, v.t. To exhibit or present to the view of others; to make known; to declare.
scriptures: Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Psa 78:6
That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: Cracow printer turned evangelical who set up a Polish press at Lyck in Masuria about 1536, translated the catechism into Polish, and served as pastor and superintendent there.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest thing to record about Małecki is that he was quarrelsome. He fought Mazvydas over translation and precedence, and the duchy's correspondence is full of his complaints. The dictionary does not smooth it over, and does not use it to cancel him either. A printing press in Masuria in 1536 was worth more to those parishes than a pleasant colleague would have been, and the Lord has generally built his church out of men who were hard to work beside.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is transmitted deliberately, down generations and through named men, and that the transmission is itself a command. The Psalm sets the duty against the natural drift of silence: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4), with the aim stated two verses on — “That the generation to come might know them” (Psa 78:6). Paul makes it a chain of four links and requires fitness at each: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). A press is one way of obeying Deuteronomy 11:19.

pos: n. (c. 1528–1553; translator of the first Polish New Testament made from the Greek, dead at about twenty-five)
etymology: Murzynowski, from the Polish village name Murzynowo; Stanisław, from Slavic stan, to stand, and slav, glory.
biblical_def: Stanisław Murzynowski was a Masovian nobleman who studied at Königsberg under Rapolionis and then at Wittenberg under Melanchthon, and went on to Italy. Back in Prussia, still in his early twenties, he translated the New Testament into Polish directly from the Greek — the first time it had been done — and Jan Seklucjan printed it at Königsberg in parts between 1551 and 1553. He wrote the preface, the marginal notes, and a Polish orthography to go with it, because the language had no settled spelling and his text needed one. He died about 1553, aged roughly twenty-five, with the complete New Testament through the press. The dictionary records him because the aim he states in his preface is John's own stated aim for writing a gospel: “But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (Joh 20:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines orthography as the art of writing words with the proper letters; a version as a translation, the rendering of a work into another language; and incorruptible as not capable of decay or dissolution.
webster_full: ORTHOGRAPHY, n. [Gr. orthos, right, and grapho, to write.] The art of writing words with the proper letters, according to common usage.
VERSION, n. [L. versio.] A translation; the rendering of a work or passage from one language into another.
INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot corrupt or decay; that cannot be bribed; incapable of dissolution.
SEED, n. The substance which contains the germ of a new plant; the principle of production; offspring.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition; methodical arrangement; a mandate; a rule.
scriptures: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
Luk 1:3
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: Translated the New Testament into Polish from the Greek, printed by Jan Seklucjan at Königsberg between 1551 and 1553; wrote the first Polish orthography to support it; died about 1553.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The notion worth correcting is that vernacular Bibles in this period were mostly made from the Latin by men content to work at second hand. Murzynowski went to the Greek, in his early twenties, and then had to invent a spelling system because Polish did not yet have one he could trust to carry the text accurately. Translation and orthography were a single job, and both were done for the sake of the text rather than the language.

The principle to recover is that the Scriptures were written with a stated purpose and that the purpose governs how they are handled. John says why he wrote: “But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name” (Joh 20:31). Luke names his method and his care — “having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3). The seed thus sown does not rot: men are born again “by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever” (1Pe 1:23), which is why a young man's short life spent on an accurate text is not wasted (Isa 40:8).

usage: “But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (Joh 20:31) — the first Polish New Testament from the Greek.
“to write unto thee in order” (Luk 1:3) — he wrote a Polish orthography so the text could be spelled consistently.
“by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever” (1Pe 1:23) — dead at about twenty-five, the work through the press.

pos: n. (c. 1530–1593; Polish-Lithuanian translator and antitrinitarian, whose learning served a denial of the deity of Christ)
etymology: Budny, a Polish surname from buda, a booth or hut; Simon, from Hebrew Shim'on, hearing.
biblical_def: Simon Budny was a Belarusian-born scholar of Hebrew, Greek and Church Slavonic who served the Radziwiłł household, worked at the press at Nesvizh, and in 1572 published at Łosk a complete Bible in Polish translated from the originals — a real feat of philology, with critical notes on the text that were ahead of their time. He was also a radical antitrinitarian. He denied the eternal deity of Christ, denied that Christ should be prayed to, questioned the virgin birth and the soul's immortality, and was excluded even by the Polish Socinians, who thought him too far gone. His notes carry his doctrine into the margins of the text he translated. The dictionary records him because he is the clearest case in this region of great learning harnessed to a lie, and the lie is answered in the first sentence of John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Antitrinitarian as one who denies the Trinity, or the existence of three persons in the Godhead; a heretic as one who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith; and the Godhead as the divine nature or essence.
webster_full: ANTITRINITARIAN, n. One who denies the Trinity, or the existence of three persons in the Godhead.
HERETIC, n. [Gr. hairetikos.] A person who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith, or to what is made the standard of orthodoxy.
GODHEAD, n. The Deity; the divine nature or essence; divinity.
WORD, n. An articulate sound expressing an idea; in Scripture, the second person in the Trinity, the Logos.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; literature; erudition.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;

And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
corruption_summary: Polish-Lithuanian Hebraist who published a complete Bible from the originals in 1572 and used its notes to deny the deity of Christ; too radical even for the Socinians, who excluded him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption in Budny is not a modern one laid on him from outside; it is his own, and it is the oldest. He had the languages, he had the manuscripts, and he worked the apparatus honestly enough that textual scholars still read his notes. Then he used the margin of his own Bible to tell its readers that the Christ of that Bible is not God. His case is the standing answer to the idea that access to the original tongues settles doctrine by itself. A man may know more Hebrew than his pastor and still not know the Lord.

The principle to recover is that the deity of the Son is not an inference the church added but the text's own first assertion: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). It is confessed by a doubting apostle to the risen Christ's face — “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28) — and Paul applies both titles to one person at his appearing: “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). John closes his letter by naming where true God and eternal life are found, and the sentence will not divide: “This is the true God, and eternal life” (1Jn 5:20).

Greek epiphaneia (G1932) — a manifestation, an appearing; Titus 2:13.
Greek alethinos (G228) — true, genuine, real; “the true God”, 1 John 5:20.
usage: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — denied in the notes of his own 1572 Bible.
“My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28) — he held that Christ is not to be prayed to.
“the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13) — excluded by the Socinians as too radical.

pos: n. (the lowland region of western Lithuania, the last part of Europe to be christened and the last to be reached by the Reformation)
etymology: A latinisation of Lithuanian Žemaitija; from zemas, low, the lowland country.
biblical_def: Samogitia is the lowland between the Nemunas and the Baltic, the last pagan region in Europe: its people were not baptised until 1413, more than a thousand years after the gospel reached Rome, and the old sacred groves and household gods survived in the countryside long after. The Reformation reached it late and thinly, and so did the Counter-Reformation; Mazvydas addressed his 1547 preface to the Lithuanians and Samogitians together because both needed a book. The bishop who finally made the region Christian in practice rather than on paper, Merkelis Giedraitis, did it in the later sixteenth century by the Reformers' own method — preaching and catechising in Samogitian, and getting the catechism printed in it. The dictionary records the region because it is Europe's own proof that the times of ignorance are long and that the command to repent is not: “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Act 17:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heathen as a pagan, one who worships idols or is unacquainted with the true God; ignorance as want of knowledge; and an inheritance as that which is or may be inherited, a possession received.
webster_full: HEATHEN, n. [Saxon haethen.] A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
IGNORANCE, n. [L. ignorantia.] Want of knowledge or instruction; unacquaintance with truth or fact.
INHERITANCE, n. That which is or may be inherited; a possession received by descent or gift.
GROVE, n. A cluster of trees; in Scripture, often a place of idolatrous worship.
UTTERMOST, a. Extreme; being in the furthest degree or at the greatest distance.
scriptures: And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
Isa 55:5
Behold, thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not, and nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee because of the LORD thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he hath glorified thee.
But as it is written, To whom he was not spoken of, they shall see: and they that have not heard shall understand.
corruption_summary: The lowland region of western Lithuania, not baptised until 1413 and catechised in its own tongue only in the later sixteenth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a romance about Samogitia that wants correcting: the last pagans of Europe as keepers of an older and gentler wisdom, christened by force and robbed of their groves. Force was indeed used, by the Order and later by the Polish crown, and the dictionary does not defend it. But the groves were not gentle, and the people themselves were not asked whether they wished to be kept as a museum. When the gospel finally came in Samogitian rather than in Latin, it was received.

The principle to recover is that long ignorance is no argument against present obligation. Paul grants the centuries of darkness and then turns on his hearers with a universal command in the present tense: “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Act 17:30). The Son's inheritance is specified as the nations out to the edge — “the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8) — and the summons goes to peoples who have no prior relation to him at all: “Behold, thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not” (Isa 55:5). Paul took that as his own charter (Rom 15:21).

pos: n. (the town on the Nevezis that became the seat and synod town of the Reformed church in Lithuania)
etymology: Kedainiai, a Lithuanian town name of disputed derivation, possibly from a personal name Kedas.
biblical_def: Kedainiai stands on the Nevezis in central Lithuania and was a Radziwiłł town. When the family went over to the Reformation in the 1550s the place became the working centre of the Lithuanian Reformed church: a stone church, a gymnasium, a press, and above all the meeting house of its synods, which gathered there repeatedly into the seventeenth century to settle doctrine, discipline, ministerial examinations and the support of parishes. Lithuanian Reformed books were printed there, and in the 1650s Daniel Klein's Lithuanian grammar and hymnal came out of the same orbit. The town's importance is almost entirely synodical: it is where the Lithuanian churches did their deciding together rather than separately. The dictionary records it for that, on the pattern of the first assembly: “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, a meeting of ministers and elders to consult on church affairs; counsel as advice, deliberation; and to consider as to think on with care, to deliberate.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. [Gr. sunodos, a coming together.] A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an ecclesiastical court.
COUNSEL, n. [L. consilium.] Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request; deliberation; consultation.
CONSIDER, v.t. [L. considero.] To think on with care; to ponder; to deliberate; to examine attentively.
ELDER, n. One who is older; in Scripture, a person who holds an office of authority in the church.
SAFETY, n. Freedom from danger or hazard; exemption from hurt; preservation from escape.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: The Radziwiłł town on the Nevezis that became the seat, school, press and synod town of the Lithuanian Reformed church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question Kedainiai raises is about patronage. The Lithuanian Reformed church was gathered, housed and paid for by one great family, and when the Radziwiłłs weakened the church weakened with them. That is a real liability in presbyterian government as much as in episcopal, and the dictionary names it: a church whose synods meet in a magnate's town may find its courage is on loan.

The principle to recover is that the churches are meant to decide together, by assembled elders, with the text open. Acts shows the shape plainly: “And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6), and the decree that follows binds consciences only in what is necessary — “to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things” (Act 15:28). Proverbs gives the reason assemblies exist, and it is not the dignity of the assembly: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). A synod is still answerable to the Scriptures its hearers are searching (Act 17:11).
